lines.note: Jinpi is a secret of a kami; the following example means revealing it. Restore initial I and the scan’s de Cami rather than do cami.

runs.text: Manifeſtar o Cami os ſegredos, ou ou

lines.note: Uaſu completes arawasu. The kami reveals secrets, or another person does so in its place; Manifeſtar corrects the damaged OCR vowel.

Tro completes outro without an inferred hyphen above; em ſeu lugar specifies acting in the kami’s place. An irregular blot above em is not a securely legible accent; no additional character is supplied.
Jinpoo is kami no takara, the kami’s treasures. The Japanese word is Camino, not the OCR’s Canino.

Jinpuu is human custom or manners. The damaged headword begins I, not F, and the final S is an upright written-register label. The second vowel of Cuſtume is worn; u is retained as the usable reading, as is the damaged final ǔ of the headword.
Jinpushoo contrasts a person of good standing with someone not counted as important. The second Japanese description continues in nu hito below.
Nu hito completes mono no kazu naranu hito. The Portuguese explicitly contrasts a noble person and a low-status person.
Jinpushoo ni yorazu means without distinction of personal standing; the Portuguese begins a formulation independent of obligations to either rank.

runs.text: nem com altos nem com baixos.

lines.note: Neither the high nor the low completes the preceding social contrast. It belongs to the same example, not a separate definition.
Jinki, hito no ki, is a person’s natural vitality. The opening Ii sequence is damaged but recoverable, not the OCR’s M.

runs.text: ¶ Itẽ, Bafo, ou ar q̃ reſulta de eſtar muita

lines.note: A second sense concerns the breath or air produced when many people are gathered. The abbreviation Itẽ and q̃ remain unexpanded.
Completes the crowded-air definition; jinki hanahada atsushi describes its heat. The scan really prints O- at the edge, despite O being a complete article.

runs.text: bafo, ou ar de muita gente he muito quente.

lines.note: The breath or air of a crowd is very hot. The first noun is bafo with f, agreeing with the earlier Bafo, not OCR baſo.

runs.text: Falta de força, ou vigor dos rins.

lines.note: Jinkyo denotes lack of strength or vitality in the kidneys, as the historical medical gloss explicitly states.
Jinkyootsuu is introduced as the first of six exceptional endowments. Both carons are visible and are not replaced by modern romanization.

runs.text: ſeis que poem os Iapoẽs que he velocidade no

lines.note: The six qualities are attributed to Japanese accounts; this one is identified as speed in movement, completed by andar on the next row.

Andar completes the speed-of-movement definition. The far-right (profunda. physically precedes the next entry but completes its Portuguese gloss; it is preserved here as displaced text, not joined to andar.
Jinri, fukaki kotowari, is a deep reason or subject. Its adjective profunda is printed at the far right of the preceding physical row.
Jinrin is equated with hito and means people. The example begins Iin- and continues into a place separated from human habitation.
Jinrin hanareta tokoro denotes a deserted or uninhabited place. The Portuguese deſpouo- continues below.
Ado completes deſpouoado de gente, devoid of inhabitants. This short line remains attached to the desert-place example.
Jinryoo comprises lands or revenue belonging to the kami. The caron is retained, and Camis is embedded in Portuguese.
Jinriki is kami no chikara, divine strength. The scan has r in the headword, not OCR t; forta- begins fortaleza below.
Completes fortaleza and adds the power of the kami. Camis belongs to the Portuguese explanation.
Jinsoo is glossed as running lightly or swiftly. The accompanying form visibly begins Vaxiri, not expected Faxiri; preserve this printed anomaly rather than silently emending it.
Jintai, explained as jin no tai, refers here to an honourable or noble person, rather than the modern anatomical sense of the homophone.
Kekkoo na jintai ja evaluates someone as a splendid personage. The Portuguese begins a description of an honourable man and continues below.
Completes homem honrado and specifies being well dressed and adorned. The clothing description explains the outward social impression.

runs.text: Caminho, ou ley da piedade, & amor

lines.note: Jintoo is the way or law of compassion and love. Its object, one’s neighbour, follows on the next line.

runs.text: do proximo, que he hũa das virtudes moraes

lines.note: Love of one’s neighbour is identified as a moral virtue; the peoples to whom the account attributes it follow below.
The Chinese and Japanese complete the description of this moral tradition. Both words here are Portuguese ethnonyms.

runs.text: Proueito, ou fruito desta virtude moral.

lines.note: Jintoku is the benefit or fruit of the preceding moral virtue. The initial I corrects OCR long s; retain the source’s fruito spelling.
Jintoona modifies a person who is modest or orderly. Its circumflex differs from the caron in the preceding Jintǒ entry and is preserved.

runs.text: deſto, quieto, ou regular, & bem criado.

lines.note: Completes modeſto and adds quiet, regular and well brought up, describing the person’s behaviour and upbringing.
Jintoorashii hito describes a dignified, modest person. The example repeats the headword, not OCR untôraxij; this is a new flush-left entry.
Grave, modest and courteous completes the preceding person-description. The entire row belongs to the Portuguese explanation.
The first Jin von is glossed fukaku tooshi, deeply remote. Its sense is temporal antiquity, not the favours of the following homographs.

runs.text: gua, & diſtante de noſſos tempos. S.

lines.note: Gua completes antigua, followed by remoteness from our times. The final upright S marks written usage.
The second Jin von denotes benefits conferred by a compassionate person. Ami- begins the description of someone disposed to do good.
Go completes amigo de bem fazer, a person inclined to beneficence. This continuation closes the second Jin von entry.
The third Jin von is fukai on, deep or great favours. It is a separate flush-left entry with its own short gloss.

runs.text: Bom homem. & amigo de bẽ fazer.

lines.note: Jinsha is a good, benevolent person. The mark after homem is a period in this impression; the abbreviation bẽ is retained.

runs.text: Eſpaço em quanto hum viue, ou està em

lines.note: Jinse denotes the duration of a person’s life or stay in this world. The final verb’s apparent grave accent is retained as eſtà.
Este mundo completes the preceding lifespan definition. It is an indented Portuguese continuation, not another temporal expression.
Jinsei is equated with the preceding lifespan term. The example begins the saying that reaching seventy has been rare since old times.

runs.text: Chegar a vida do homem atè os

lines.note: Mare nari completes the Japanese saying. The Portuguese translation begins “for human life to reach,” followed by the age below.

runs.text: 70. ainda antiguamente foi couſa rara. S.

lines.note: The scan prints the numeral 70, not OCR vo. The translation says this was rare even in antiquity; the final S is upright.
Jinseki, hito no ato, denotes human footprints or traces. The Portuguese complement follows on the next row.
Completes footprints of people. Jinseki tayeta tokoro introduces a place where human traces have ceased; Lu- begins lugar below.

runs.text: gar por onde não paſſa gente nem raſto de ho-

lines.note: Describes a place through which no people pass and where no human tracks remain; the word homem divides at ho-.

runs.text: mem, ou lugar inhabitado, e deſerto.

lines.note: Mem completes homem. The alternative explanation is an uninhabited, deserted place, preserving Portuguese inhabitado and the printed conjunction e.
Jinshin is hito no kokoro, the human heart or mind. The scan’s initial I is not the OCR’s lowercase l.
Jinshu is a lord or master. This short complete entry is distinct from both the preceding human-heart term and the following remedy.
Jinyaku is a remedy for the kidneys. The initial I replaces OCR long s; Mezinha retains the historical medical vocabulary.
Jin’ei, hito no kage, is a person’s shadow or figure. The Portuguese extends the sense beyond a literal shadow below.

runs.text: aparencia, ou vulto de homem que aparece

lines.note: Adds the appearance or outline of a person who becomes visible, with the distance qualification on the next row.
De longe means at a distance and completes the description of the human figure. It is indented body text.
Jin’en yuubi is paraphrased as deep, remote and subtle. Retain the printed Fucacu spelling and grave over u rather than regularizing them.
The Portuguese gives lofty and profound; the Japanese example begins the same expression modifying kotowari below.
Kotowari completes the example of a profound reason or proposition. The paired Portuguese nouns explain the intended intellectual sense.
Copioſa adds abundance or richness to the proposition’s depth. The final S is an upright written-register label.
Jinzui is kami no mizzu, water of the kami. Cami occurs within the Portuguese definition; the example follows below.
Jinzui wo nomu means drinking this sacred liquid. Portuguese allows water or wine, with the ritual setting continued below.

runs.text: diante do Cami como juramento, ou promeßa

lines.note: The liquid is drunk before the Cami as an oath or promise; Cami is the Japanese divine being within the Portuguese explanation, not a new entry.
Completes the promise to observe or keep some undertaking. The tilde in algũa and the final period remain visible inside the crop.

runs.text: Hum dos ſeis dotes, que eſcreueo

lines.note: Jinzuu denotes a supernatural faculty, here one of six gifts described by Xaca. The Japanese name begins with upright Xa at the end of this physical line and continues below; no unprinted hyphen is added.

runs.text: ca, como ſutileza. ¶ Itẽ, Sabeduria ma-

lines.note: The opening ca completes Xaca from the preceding row. After the example of subtlety, the paragraph introduces a further sense, superhuman knowledge; the printed ma- divides mais across the next row.

runs.text: is que humana com que hum ſabe as couſas diſ-

lines.note: Continues the definition of knowledge exceeding ordinary human ability, allowing one to know distant things. Preserve both the initial is completing mais and the final diſ-.
Completes distant and absent things, then begins the alternative expressions Iinzzǔ, l, jinzzuriqiuo vru. The lower-case j after the alternative marker is printed, and its word continues after jinz-.
Completes jinzzuriqiuo vru, acquiring the supernatural power; the Portuguese states receiving this gift. The zuriqiuo continuation belongs to the preceding example, not a separate headword.
Iinzzuriqi is a separate headword for the same supernatural power. Idem explicitly refers back to the preceding entry and its acquisition formula.
Jippoo is explained by macotono nori, true law, matching Ley verdadeira. Both the headword and Japanese synonym are upright; the circumflex on ô is retained.
The first two upright letters read Ii, not long-s, giving Iippon. Fino moto, origin of the sun, is explained as the east and then Japan; the historical form is not modernized to Nippon.
Iippu, truth or falsity, is unpacked by macoto ya ina ya, whether true or not. Restore the upright Ii initial from the scan and retain the terminal fal-.
The example cotono jippuga xirenu says that the truth of a matter is not known. The Portuguese translation starts with A-, continued as inda below; the preceding ſidade completes falſidade.

runs.text: inda ſe não ſabe de certo a verdade, ou mẽtira.

lines.note: Completes Ainda and explains that the truth or lie is not yet known for certain. Keep the abbreviation mẽtira and the printed sequence de certo rather than modernizing orthography.
Iippuuo qijte maitta means coming after hearing the facts or certainty of the matter. The printed qijte has two dotted vowel letters; the Portuguese begins Ouuindo a cer-.
Completes certeza do que paßa vim: the speaker came upon hearing what was actually happening. This is the translation of the preceding Japanese example, not a new entry.

runs.text: Varela de Bonzos com ermidas, ou cellas

lines.note: Iiqe, a Buddhist temple establishment, is described as a temple of Bonzos with hermitages or cells. Varela is part of the Portuguese gloss, and the description continues below.

runs.text: ao redor dentro da meſma cerca.

lines.note: The surrounding hermitages or cells lie inside the same enclosure. This completes the temple-establishment definition, with the final period and enclosing right rule visible.
Iiqen is firsthand seeing: mizzucara miru, seeing for oneself. The scan has upright Ii rather than the provisional ti; Mizzucara keeps its printed double z.
The example joins firsthand seeing with personal understanding, matching Ver, & entender por ſi. Restore Ii at the start while preserving jitocu and the long ſ in ſuru.
The scan includes a paragraph sign omitted by the draft before Iiqen gacumon. The phrase concerns independent study; the Portuguese continues into the next row.
Completes the explanation of studying by oneself: reading without a teacher. The inherited mestre spelling is retained without resolving the difficult italic st ligature by automatic normalization.
Iiqiô is affectionate instruction, expressed by itçucuximi voxiye. The initial is upright Ii, not long-s; preserve the headword circumflex and the cedilla in the Japanese synonym.

runs.text: como a do pay pera com o filho.

lines.note: The comparison is a father’s loving instruction of his child. The Portuguese pay and pera are historical spellings and remain unchanged.

Iiqi, food or eating, is equated with xocu. The example Iiqiuo ſugoſu concerns excess in eating; its translation begins with the visibly capitalized italic Co- at the right edge, not lower-case roman co-.
The opening mer completes Comer demaſiadamente, eating too much. The next paragraph introduces Iiqiuo tomuru, stopping someone’s eating or food supply.
The gloss means preventing someone from eating. Iiqidomeuo ſuru is then supplied as an equivalent expression; preserve the visible tilde in alguẽ and the terminal ſu-.
The opening ru completes ſuru from the preceding line; Idem gives the same food-withholding meaning. This short physical continuation is fully included in its crop.

Iiqidǒ is a dining hall or refectory. Restore the upright Ii initial and the caron on ǒ. The central Portuguese types are worn, especially the open-looking o, but Refeitorio remains the usable reading after enlargement.
Iiqidome is referred back to Iiqi, where withholding food has just been illustrated. Vide is italic apparatus, while the referenced Japanese headword Iiqi is upright, including its initial I.

Iiqigo means after eating; the dictionary prefers Xocugo and supplies xocuno nochi. The entry is flush left, not a continuation. Preserve the grave in Meliùs and the unhyphenated De at the right edge.
The opening pois completes De pois de comer, the explanation of after eating. There is no lost further body row here: the separate Iiqi- below is the page catchword.
